[Question: Why is it that the kidneys alone are two? [Answer: It is because the kidneys are not both kidneys. That which is on the left is the kidney;
that which is on the right is the Gate of Life (mingmen). The Gate of Life is the abode of all the spirit and essence, and the point where the original qi (yuanqi) is bound.
Therefore, men store the essence (*jing*) therein, while women bind the fetus (*bao*) therein; thus we know that the kidneys are one.
As for "like following and examining the leaves," the *Nan jing* reads "like following and pulling the leaves. Furthermore, according to Xu Shi’s compilation of the *Huangdi mai jing*:
"In spring, Wood reigns as the sovereign; its pulse is taut, fine, and long—this is the normal pulse. Pulse...
If the pulse is instead loose like a string, yet feels slightly rough and short, this is the Lung overcoming the Liver; it is metal carving wood.

This constitutes a rebellious and perverse transgression, and in ten cases out of ten, death will follow without cure. In summer, the Heart-fire reigns, and its pulse is floating, large, and dispersed; this is the normal pulse.
If, instead, one obtains a pulse that is deep, soft, and short, this is the Kidney overcoming the Heart; it is water carving fire.
Fire [the heart] is the great rebellion of a thief and evil. If one dies from this, it is incurable.

In the Central Palace, when the Earth element—the Spleen pulse—is dominant, a pulse that is "a-a" (deep and slow) is the normal pulse. If, conversely, it is obtained as stringy, thin, and long, this is the Liver overcoming the Spleen;
Wood comes to carve Earth. This is the great rebellion of a thief and evil. If one dies from this, it is incurable. In autumn, the Metal element—the Lungs—is dominant.
Regarding the pulse: one that is faintly floating, short, and wiry is the normal pulse. Its appearance is floating and light, like the down on a bird’s back being ruffled by a gentle breeze.
If, instead, it is floating, large, and forceful, this indicates that the Heart has overpowered the Lungs; fire is carving wood, which constitutes a "thieving" pathogen and a major rebellion.
This results in death within ten days and cannot be cured. In winter, when the Water element of the Kidneys reigns, its pulse is deep and soft.
If the pulse is slippery or firm and solid, with drops like water leaking from a roof onto a stone, this is the normal (ping) pulse.

Conversely, if it is obtained as large and slow, this indicates that the spleen has invaded the kidneys; earth overcomes water, constituting a "thieving" pathogenic factor. Such a case will die within ten days and cannot be cured.
When the spleen pulse arrives, it is like a thread; [the character "he" (何) is an error and should be "a" (阿)].
Wang Shu-he’s *Pulse Decisions* (*Mai jue*) says: "A-a; slow as spring willows. This is the spleen abiding in the four seasons."
The commentary explains that *lun* (論) is pronounced with the *xi* (習) radical and the *si* (思) radical; it means minor pain.
Regarding *ji-li* (擊攊), the *Zhi-gui* (指歸) states that it refers to tickling under a person's armpits with the hand, causing them to feel a sense of dread and itchiness, which makes them laugh.
The character [豸*童] in "師子[豸*童][豸*童]" is an error; it should be written as [泳-永+董]. This refers to breast milk.
For example, fermenting wine where the dregs become turbid and turn into filth is the metaphor; the eight characters following "dregs and turbidity" represent the Dharma.
Dregs are like excrement; wine is like urine.

The treatise states: If one generates heavy contact, and the inhalation and exhalation repeatedly enter and exit in accordance with the earth element, it is heavy; if the inhalation and exhalation are contrary to one another, it results in illness.
Its sovereign was Taihao (pronounced *hào*). This was the Lord Fuxi.
Guming (the first character pronounced with the ancient *hóu* rhyme) was the son of Taihao;
he was Yan Di, the Lord Shen Nong.
Zhurong was none other than Chongli. He assisted Emperor Yu and performed meritorious service; his brilliance illuminated the world. Emperor Yu bestowed upon him the title "Zhurong.
Zhurong signifies "brightly illuminating."
Shao Mao was the Lord of Jintian; he was the son of the Yellow Emperor.
Rufou was the son of Shao Mao.
Zhuanxu was the Lord of Gaoyang.
Xuanming and Shaohao had two sons named Xu and Xi.
Huangdi Xuan-yun’s son was Hou-tu Zhuan-xu’s son, named Li;
he served as the official of the Earth. Together with the five sovereigns and five ministers, they were all [enlightened].
He established virtue and meritorious deeds before the time of Yao; those who now possess the empire worship him as a deity.
The character *lǜ* (腭) is pronounced with the *gē* (各) and *qiè* (切) finals; it should instead be written as *yù* (齶), meaning the "palate" (*tǔ yù*).
One should treat this as a discussion on the origins of symptoms rather than a mere inquiry.
One must not conflict with a single person seated above; "seated above" (yī shàng) refers to what the laity call sitting upon the head of another.
If the breath is coarse, this constitutes a conflict.
To supplement the breath within the nostrils so that it becomes cool, clear, peaceful, and harmonious is what constitutes "supplementation.
There are four sounds of the breath: *qi* (vital energy), *chuǎn* (panting), and two others as its attendants; these three are not the primary element. The primary element is the breath itself.
In the arrangement of the skeletal joints (*asthi-saṃdhi*), *jie* (jie) should be read as *jie* (joint).
*Long* (long) should be read as *long* (lóng), meaning "hazy" (*ménglóng*).
*Jingzhi* (jingzhi) carries the sense of "startled leaping. *Zhi* (zhi) is not clearly defined.
The Shadow of a Snake on a Wall. According to the *Book of Jin*, Yue Yanfu had a close guest who did not come for a long time.

When Yanfu asked the reason, the guest replied: "Previously, while sitting at your table, I was honored with a gift of wine. Just as I was about to drink, I saw a snake in my cup. I felt very ill at ease about it, and after drinking, I fell ill.
Yanfu said, "At that time, there was a horned bow on the wall of the Henan hall; the snake was merely the reflection of the bow's horns."
A lacquer vessel was painted with a snake. Yanfu thought that the snake in his cup was actually the reflection of a horned bow.
He then set out wine at the same spot as before and said to his guest, "Is there anything else you see in the wine? The guest replied, "What I see is exactly as it was before.
Yanfu explained the reason for this, and the guest’s mind was suddenly enlightened; his chronic illness was instantly cured.
Medicinal herbs and medicine are treated like firewood.
*Zhi yue* (治噦): pronounced with the second tone on *yue*, it refers to the upward reversal of qi (*qi-ni*).
*Bao ru* (暴汝): pronounced with the second tone on *pu*, it means to expose. Having buried [the herbs] at a dog’s tooth-deep depth in a sunny location, the incantation says:
"If it does not heal, I shall expose you to the elements.

When the master carpenter Zhuge [Zhuge] laid down his axe at the site of Yingren—*jin* (釿) should be read as *jin* (斤), meaning an adze—Yingren was a man of great skill, and thus those who could match him were few.
Song Yu addressed the King of Chu, saying: "There was a guest who sang in the city of Ying. At its beginning..."
It is said that when he sang the "Xialiren" and "Baren," thousands of people in the capital joined in harmony.
When he sang the "Yang'a" and "Xuelu," several hundred people in the capital joined in harmony. When he sang the "Yangchun" and "Baixue," only a few dozen people in the capital joined in harmony.
When he modulated the *shang* and *yu* notes and intermingled them with the flowing *zhong*, the people of the capital [joined in harmony].
Yet those who could harmonize with it did not exceed a few people. Thus, the more sublime the melody, the fewer those who could harmonize with it.

Commentary: "Obtaining perspiration" is taken as the measure; one must concentrate their will with such intensity that it is like a patient obtaining perspiration, which clearly indicates the illness has been cured.
"Qin dudu" should be written as "xian.
Do not say "kou-zhai"; "kou-zhai" should be written as "yan-pao," meaning clamor or shouting.

"Various obstacles arise like peaks": the height of the obstacles is like the rising of many mountain peaks; alternatively, it may simply be the character *fēng* (peak/edge), as in "arising like the edge of a blade.
As the *Wénxuǎn* says: "Right and wrong arise like sharp edges (*fēngqǐ*)."
*Bǎng* (bǎng) is pronounced with the *bù* (步) and *xíng* (行) finals. In the *Hànshū*, Guō Shèrén said to the Emperor of Hàn:
"I wish to have Dōngfāng Chuò perform a 'covered shooting' (*fùshè*). If Chuò hits the mark, I shall be punished with one hundred *bǎng*. Yán Sīgǔ’s commentary states: "*Bǎng* means to strike."
The character "zhē" (遮) also serves as a phonetic loan for "yāo" (邀).
In the phrase "yào jūn" (要君), "yāo" is pronounced with the initial *y*. "Wúshàng" (無上) means that there is nothing more honored than it.
In the twenty-eighth year of Duke Xī of the *Zuǒzhuan*, winter, Duke Wén of Jìn summoned the Son of Heaven to a meeting at Wēn and caused the feudal lords to pay him court.
Zhongni said, "To summon a ruler by means of a minister cannot serve as a model for instruction. The Book of Documents says, 'The Heavenly King went hunting at Heyang.
This was a stratagem employed by the Marquis of Jin."

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*)... [This] was already cited in the second fascicle; the commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa* has finished its explanation.
Since the Master of the Record (Ji-zhu) stated that one who studies the Buddha-dharma must not be entirely deluded, please consult the previous notes again.

The eleven pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) are termed "pervasive causes" (*sarvatragahetu*). These consist of the five views and doubt belonging to the level of suffering (*duḥkha*), as well as false view, adherence to views, and ignorance (*avidyā*) belonging to the level of origin (*samudaya*).
Ignorance is none other than delusion (*moha*); thus, there are exactly eleven.
Regarding the phrase "clothes are tattered" (*lánlǚ*), it should be written as *lánlǜ*.
The character *bó* (縛) is pronounced with the *qì* (去) tone, meaning "to bind tightly.
The character *jiàn* (間) is pronounced with the *qùshēng* (去聲) tone, meaning "to instigate strife and cause estrangement."
*Jiàn-rǎn*: the pronunciation of *jiàn* is like *jiān*; it carries the meaning of soaking or immersing.
The ten dharmas for verification appear in the text below. *Chàn*:
pronounced with the *chū* and *lián* finals combined.

As long as it has not been relinquished or lost, the discipline exists spontaneously and constantly. Regarding the relinquishment of the precepts according to the Vinaya: one uses speech to communicate to the mind, thereby abandoning the essence of the original undertaking.
One should perform the ritual in the presence of another, saying once: "I, the bhikṣu [Name], relinquish the precepts of the Three Jewels, the preceptor, the teacher, and the training matters.
Upon this single utterance, the essence ceases to exist. As for the loss of the precepts: it occurs through the arising of wrong views or the loss of the wearing [of the robes].
If one wears both male and female sexual organs, the Dharma is lost and extinguished. However, prior to its relinquishment or loss, the substance of the precepts remains ever-present;
this is what is meant by "wholesome non-informative action" (*kuśala-avijñapti*). As for "unwholesome non-informative action," it is like possessing instruments of slaughter:
although one has not yet killed an animal, the unwholesome offense remains ever-present and continues to exist in a continuous stream.

Regarding "simultaneous with the action" (kriyā-saha) non-informative action (avijñapti), the *Karma-siddhi-śāstra* states: "At the time of the action, the action is present while the agent is absent;

this is 'simultaneous with the action' non-informative action. Both of these are causes of the precept (*śīla*). Upon the completion of the third *karmavācanā*, the karma is fulfilled, and both types of precepts are perfected;

hence it is called "simultaneous with the action" non-informative action. This does not preclude the existence of "concomitant with the body" (*rūpa-saha*) non-informative action, which nonetheless arises subsequently. Furthermore, there are many [instances].
The Treatise says: For example, when one performs the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—they arise simultaneously with the preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Later, if one violates the teachings and breaks the precepts, as well as contravenes the fundamental vow (*yāma*;
here pronounced *yào*, meaning a vow maintained for the duration of one's life), [the consequences follow].
In the *Chanmen chanboluomi* (The Chan Gate’s Perfection of Dhyāna), it says:
"Youluo" (遊邏邏)—the second character is pronounced with a departing tone (*qùshēng*)—means to patrol.
The official who oversees mountains and marshes is the present-day Minister of the Department of Forests (*Yúbù láng*).
The eighty-four thousand dharma-gates are its hair; the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is its topknot; the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is its head;
great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is its eyes; the untainted (*anāsrava*) is its nose; the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are its mouth;
the forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are its teeth; the two types of wisdom (*jñāna*) are its hands; the Tathāgatagarbha is its abdomen; and the three samādhis are its waist.
If one takes the principle as the primary object of focus, it cannot remedy evil; if one examines these two [aspects] closely, they appear as if their meaning and force are insufficient.

If one adds a single phrase, saying, "one must observe both retribution and [the principle]," only then will the meaning become manifest. Therefore, the *Soyao* states: "The term 'dharma-gate' (dharmaparyāya) implies that its meaning encompasses both form and retribution."
They are not called Bodhisattvas; they are all termed "works of Māra. This summarizes the preceding text:
that is to say, if one speaks of an evil Māra who manifests in forms such as a Buddha and so forth to destroy the six perfections, such a person is not called a Bodhisattva.

Regarding the remaining four penetrations (*abhijñā*), they are explained as before; for example, the penetration of *bodhi*, *dharma*, and *jñāna* applies to both the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and the *bodhisattva*.
Those that correspond to the four names within the realm are: namely, one, five, and six, combined with two, three, and four, which together constitute the realm.
Regarding the "inner four māras":
the characters *zhui* (怡-台+追) and *ti* (愓) do not appear in the rhyme dictionaries. Ancient scholars all read them as *tui* (堆) and *ti* (逖).
In the *Xiǎozhǐguān* (小止觀), they are read as *tuī* (推) and *tī* (剔).
*Jiū* (啾) is pronounced with the *qián* (千) and *jié* (結) finals.
Regarding "thin gold leaf" (*jīnbó*), the second character "bó" (薄) should likely be "chuán" (傳), as in "applying powder" (*fùfěn*).

Various kinds of non-timely drinks (*zhǒngzhǒng fēishí jiāng*) are those that are considered "non-timely" after noon. The Buddha permitted the drinking of such drinks, specifically referring to sugarcane juice (*gānzhè jiāng*).
Grape juice and so forth.
*Fúyì* (伏翼) refers to a bat; [the character] *biān* (蝙) is used as a variant.
*Hé* (貉)—the second character is pronounced with the *xià* (下) and *gē* (各) finals—should correctly be written as *dú* (貈). It is a beast resembling a fox that is fond of sleep.
The character 獦 (gè) is pronounced jué and means "to dispatch. The *Sōyào* states: "Today in Jiangdong, the wild boar (*pí*) is called 獦 (gè). The character 豼 (pí) is pronounced bì."
It is a fierce beast belonging to the category of tigers and cubs.
The female is called *zhǐ*. According to the *Sòuyào*, it is pronounced with the initial *bù*.
*Chū* (pronounced like *shū*). A large variety of tiger. *Chì-yǔ*:
the first character is pronounced *ā-bā* (cut by *wū-bā*), the second is pronounced *yǔ*. The *Erya* states: "The *chì-yǔ* is a species of beast;
it has claws like a tiger, eats humans, and runs with great speed."
In the *Zhi guan fu xing zhuan hong jue*, fascicle 14, it says:

"From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the ten abodes (*vihāra*), Māra cannot speak of the Perfect [Teaching]. Regarding the mention of "the first stage and so forth," this refers to the distinct-vehicle stages (*bhedabhūmi*) and the perfect-vehicle abodes (*pūrṇavihāra*).
Other passages simply state that [Māra] speaks of the stages prior to the distinct-vehicle stages.
Regarding the term "jiǎo zhì" (狡擲), it is likely a scribal error for "huá" (猾).

It is not yet clear whether the stage of the "seeing-position" (見位) in the Shared Teaching (通教) corresponds to the stage of "subduing" (伏) and "seeing" (見) in the Tripitaka Teaching, or whether it is simply a transcription error.
Treatise: The preceding four sections explain the contemplation of impurity for those with much greed, up to the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* and the *Ṣaṭtriṃśatkleśamala-sūtra* consist of two fascicles. The upper fascicle clarifies that the thirty-six proclivities (*anuśaya*) constitute the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):

ten proclivities belong to the category of origination (*samudaya*), seven each to cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), and two proclivities to the category of the path, to which four types of reflection (*vitarka*) are added.

It is likely that this refers to the thirty-six *kleśas* (defilements) as they appear in the *Vimala-nāma-sūtra*. Since the meaning of "defilement" (*mòu*) and "affliction" (*shǐ*) is identical, it is permissible to cite them here.

Within the nine meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), both the phenomenal and the noumenal are present; however, they are distinguished as Mahayana or Hinayana based on whether they pertain to one's own practice or to the transformation of others.
As it is said: "The preliminary practice for a bodhisattva consists of hearing and reflection. One establishes the mind single-pointedly in mundane and supramundane virtues;

whether through calm abiding (*śamatha*) or insight (*vipaśyanā*), one is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Body and mind come to rest in supreme quiescence... (and so forth). Regarding the objective:
as in benefiting sentient beings, the bodhisattva within meditative concentration relies upon the act of giving to sentient beings according to what is meaningful.
Benefiting others, engaging in the same activities as them, and eliminating their various sufferings;

that which should be explained regarding knowing gratitude and repaying kindness, protecting against all terrors, and freeing them from all sorrows and pains, and so forth—these nine dhyānas are all the unique dhyānas of the Bodhisattva.
The followers of the two vehicles do not even hear its name. Now, taking one's own practice as "small" and transforming others as "great," this applies likewise to those prior to the eighth stage.
If, after the eighth stage, those of inferior capacity are received and introduced into the middle [vehicle], [it is likewise].
This is indeed objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*).

According to the treatise, there are twelve gates for one's own practice and twelve gates for transforming others; these are the twelve gates of dhyāna for praising the Dharma and the praiser, whether practiced by oneself or [taught to others].
"Or it may encourage others to practice. 'Praising the Dharma' refers to praising the dharmas of the various branches of the forest [of merit].
'Praising the gates' refers to praising the twelve gates. 'Praising dhyāna' refers to praising meditative concentration."
It is said that only after the Five Wheels of Meditation (*pañca-cakra-dhyāna*) can the characteristics and natures of good and evil be verified.

Furthermore, it is stated: "Now, through the practice of *śamatha*, one realizes the Five Wheels. First is the Earth Wheel (*pṛthivī-cakra*): by means of *śamatha*, the merits of the first dhyāna are produced, just as the earth gives rise to all things.
Second is the Water Wheel (*ap-cakra*): if, within the Earth Wheel, one realizes the water-wheel samādhi, then the merits of the various dhyānas are immediately manifested. Third...

The wind-wheel: samādhi corresponds to the semblance stage of outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), and its manifestation marks entry into the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). The fourth, the sand-gold wheel:
this bodhisattva enters among the ranks of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood, destroying the dust-like afflictions (*kleśa*).

The fifth, the diamond wheel: through samādhi, all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are severed; within the bodhisattva’s mind, subtle delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*) are destroyed. This is the verbal testimony.
Regarding the "Root-Nature of Good and Evil": following the Five Wheels, the text states that there are four ways to examine the root-nature of good and evil:
first, the chapter on wholesome dharmas; second, the signs of the arising of wholesome roots; third, the reality or unreality [of those signs]; and fourth, the process of discernment.
As well as the nature of external paths (*bāhyatīrthika*), the nature of the world (*lokadhātu-svabhāva*),
the nine pairs, and— as mentioned in the preceding text— the sequential and non-sequential, the mixed and unmixed, up to the "further" and "not further," and so forth.
Therefore, they are not included at all within the nine pairs, nor is "attention" (manasikāra) included at all.
That these—cultivation (bhāvanā) and production (utpāda)—are combined into sixteen phrases has already been annotated in the seventh previous record.

Now, regarding the text on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there are twelve phrases concerning the cultivation of principle through phenomena (*li xiu shi fa*), the cultivation of phenomena through principle (*shi fa li fa*), and the cultivation of both principle and phenomena (*li shi liu fa*).

There are, however, four phrases concerning the cultivation of non-principle and non-phenomena (*fei li fei shi xiu*), the cultivation of phenomena through phenomena (*shi xiu shi fa*), and the cultivation of both phenomena through phenomena (*shi xiu shuang yi fa*).

Regarding the cultivation of phenomena (*dharma*), there are four permutations of "neither-nor" arising; regarding the cultivation of principle (*li*), there are likewise four permutations; and regarding the simultaneous cultivation of both, there are also four permutations.

Now, within this [text on] *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, these twelve permutations do not exist. There are only cases such as: the cultivation of neither-phenomenon-nor-principle giving rise to phenomenon-arising, up to and including the cultivation of neither-phenomenon-nor-principle giving rise to neither-phenomenon-nor-principle-arising.
In the commentary [on the character *míng*], the character *míng* (clear/pure) does not appear; I suspect it is merely the character *hù* (sudden). [Yí-lì]:
the first character is pronounced *lì-dǒng* (cut by force); the second has the sound *lì*. It means to be frequently malicious.
There are those who possess long-standing desire, long-standing non-arrival, and long-standing duration.

In each and every joint, there are aspects that are both deviant and correct, as in the case of cultivation and realization; as within fundamental dhyāna, there are eight tactile sensations (*spraṣṭavya*).

Within these tactile sensations, there are ten pairs of deviant characteristics: first, the substance of touch; second, concentration and distraction; third, emptiness and existence; fourth, light and darkness; fifth, sorrow and joy.
Sixth, suffering and pleasure; seventh, good and evil; eighth, folly and wisdom; ninth, bondage and liberation; tenth, strength and weakness. As for the correct characteristics:

first, the characteristic of contact according to the Dharma; second, the characteristic of concentration; third, the characteristic of emptiness; fourth, the characteristic of clarity; fifth, the characteristic of joy; sixth, the characteristic of bliss.
The seven marks of goodness, the eight marks of knowledge, the nine liberations, and the tenfold mental composure—all these are in accordance with the Dharma.
As it is with one dhyāna, so it is with all dhyānas.
The pure form (*rūpa*) of the desire realm exists above the various sense organs; the ultimate sense organs (*paramārtha-indriya*) exist above the physical sense organs (*prātibhāsika-indriya*).
"Liao-luan" and "liao-ying" should be read as "liao.
"Re-zhuo" (熱[榷-木+月])—the character [榷] is pronounced with the *ke* and *qie* finals combined—is a type of meat broth.
The character *sō* (鯖) means to boil fish and meat; it is also written as *sei* (膾).
According to traditional interpretation, it refers to the four realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and their four corresponding [afflictions].
It signifies a state of desolation, lacking boundaries, and profound obscurity.

In terms of substantial entities, there are only ten. Since the first, second, and third dhyānas share the same factor of bliss (*sukha*), one should not speak of the first, second, and third as having distinct factors of bliss.
Consequently, they should not be expanded into eighteen or eleven factors.
First, the cultivation of skillful means; second, the realization of the signs of intermediate realization. Regarding the sixth, the signs of the arising of the first dhyāna, it is explained:
"The practitioner realizes sixteen kinds of accomplishments within the stage of *anāgamya* (the threshold concentration); these are the signs of the arising of the first dhyāna. As for the sixteen:"
That is to say: motion, itching, coolness, warmth, lightness, heaviness, roughness, smoothness; furthermore: agitation, tranquility, cold, heat, buoyancy, sinking, hardness, and softness.
The meaning of the "two branches" is analyzed as follows: just as from the roots of a tree there arise branches and twigs.
Third, regarding the essence and function of cause and effect: the internal and external skillful means, as well as the stage of non-attainment (*anāgamya*), constitute the cause;

the realization of the first dhyāna constitutes the result. Furthermore, the five factors (*pañcāṅga*) serve as the cause, while the sixth—the essence of silent concentration (*tūṣṇīmbhāva-samādhi*)—is the result. This is the essence.

Regarding "function" (*vṛtti*): one takes the mind of silence itself as the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). From the contact of silence until its initial arousal, the five factors constitute the function.

Function arises from the essence; thus, the function follows after [the essence]. Furthermore, when the dharma of the five factors arises as the fruit of silence, this takes silence as the essence and the five factors as the function.
The four clarifications regarding the depth and shallowness of the Buddha’s disciples practicing various meditations consist of three grades—lower, middle, and upper.
Beyond these three grades, there are nine grades. If discussed in detail, there should be immeasurable grades.
Regarding the five types of progress and regression when realizing the first dhyāna, there are four kinds of persons whose faculties and natures differ:
namely, those subject to regression (*hāna-bhāgīya*), those who abide (*sthiti-bhāgīya*), those who progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*), and those who lead to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*).

As for those subject to regression, when a person attains the first dhyāna, they may lose it due to some cause or even without any cause. Those who abide do not regress. Those who progress, whether or not they apply effort...

The "universal clarity" (*sāmānya-vidyā*) mentioned in the Great Sūtra refers to the universal clarity of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). It exists in those with roots of goodness but not in those who are icchantikas;

Because no new [defilements] are produced, both the agent and the object are exhausted; thus, what was previously recorded as "being made to act" (niyuktatva)—meaning that the afflictions are the agents and the fruits are the objects acted upon—is now such that the agents have reached their end.
The *Hétú* was borne [by a tortoise]; the diagrams emerged from the Yellow River and the Luo River. The inscription read: "A numinous tortoise bore a book;
its shell was vermilion and its markings were azure. It appeared among the *qí* shrubs. *Qí* is a type of herb; this plant grows in Cāizhōu.
Wherever *qí* grass appears upon the ground, there must be a numinous tortoise beneath it.
The *Shèguīyīn* (攝龜音) states that its abdominal shell can expand and contract of its own accord, and it is fond of eating snakes.
Throughout the ten sections, the *Sanzàng* (三藏), *Sānshèng* (三乘), *Fāngděng* (方等), and *Tōngjiào* (通教) treatises above clarify these matters;

when it says "śrāvaka" and "pratyekabuddha," it clarifies both vehicles in general, and when it says "bodhisattva," it generally indicates all three vehicles. Upon reaching this point, one should reflect.

Within the *Yi jing* (Treatise on the Profound Meaning), the Three Baskets (*Tripitaka*) are clarified. While the Three Baskets encompass all three vehicles (*triyāna*), they are subsequently presented separately; specifically, the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and Bodhisattvas are distinguished within the Shared Teaching (*paryāyaśāsana*).
The *Souyao* states: "The general and the specific are applied according to convenience; they cannot be standardized in a single way."
Furthermore, two additional categories are established separately outside of these two: "gradual-tardy" and "sudden-tardy. The text states:

"If one is gradual-tardy, the afflictions of the fourth stage are first eliminated prior to the initial stage. If one is sudden-tardy, the five stages are completely subdued prior to the initial stage."
"Having ascended to the [first] abode, one completely destroys the five abodes. Jingxi criticized this, saying: "The four abodes prior to the first abode have already been eliminated.

The scriptural citations belong to the Perfect [Teaching], and this is the case everywhere; even up to 'having ascended to the abode and completely destroying,' this immediately reveals that the five abodes prior to the [first] abode were entirely present.
He further stated: "It is 'sudden-sudden,' like the purification of the six sense organs in the *Lotus Sūtra*, which does not say they were previously severed."

The realization and severance of *dṛṣṭi-kleśa* (delusions of view) and *bhāvanā-kleśa* (delusions of cultivation) are both sudden. Regarding the "gradual-sudden" [approach], the *Ratnaketu-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states that one is "permanently parted from the ocean of the wheel of suffering," which means first eliminating the delusions of view and cultivation.

Furthermore, it is criticized as being self-contradictory to claim otherwise. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the phrase "untainted faculty of mind" (*anāsrava-manas-indriya*) and in the *Ratnaketu-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, the phrase "permanently parted from the ocean of suffering"—between "untainted" (*anāsrava*) and "parted" (*viyukta*), there is merely a distinction between cause and effect.
"Bai yingying" (White Yingying) should be written as "ying" (brilliant); it is the same as "ziying" (purple brilliance) mentioned below.

One should consider that "guanjian guan" (Contemplation for Dispelling Anger) should be written as "huan" (joy). It is the name of a herb; it is so named because when consumed, it removes a person's anger and resentment.
It grows in the mountain valleys of Yizhou in Xichuan. Its leaves resemble those of the soapberry (*gleditsia sinensis*).
The *xuān* (pronounced xuān) grass, known as "forgetting sorrow" (*wàngyōu*), is the same as the *lùcōng* (deer-onion). Those who consume it eliminate human sorrow.
These two sentences originate from Xi Kang’s *Yǎngshēng lùn* (Treatise on Nourishing Life); their explanation is identical to that in Zhang Hua’s *Bówù zhì* (Monograph on the Wonders of Nature).
The character "chóng" (重) should be "lóu" (樓);
thus, as in "three vehicles" (三車), it should be "zhī" (知).
"Zhèng zhèng kōng jiàn" (正證空見) should correctly be "yǐn" (引).
*Zhi guan fu xing chuan hong jue zhu lan*, Scroll Four (End).
Postscript to the Three Great Works (by Youyan):
In the past, I served as the abbot for three successive terms. Later, finding myself incapable of leading the assembly, I consequently built a hermitage for myself.
Although he was thus situated [in the world], he possessed the aspiration to support and uphold the religious teachings, wishing to establish a vast cause for merit.
He produced the *Beijian* (Complete Examination) in four fascicles as a commentary on the *Fahua xuanyi*; the *Jiannan* (Annotated Difficulties) in five fascicles as a commentary on the *Wenju ji*;

and the *Zuolan* (Aided Reading) in four fascicles as a commentary on the *Zhiguan fuxing chuanhong jue*. For over twenty years, he had personally opened and scrutinized these works with his own eyes; though his mind was exhausted...

Though his body was afflicted by illness, he daily immersed himself in the Dharma-flower Ocean of Nature (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-svabhāva-sāgara*), never daring to complain of weariness. Thereupon, he made this vow:
"May I rely upon the merit of these auxiliary practices so that my spirit may be reborn in Sukhāvatī and quickly realize the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).

May I manifest bodies throughout the ten directions, throughout the limits of the future, constantly propagating the True Dharma to guide and instruct sentient beings, causing all beings to open the Buddha-wisdom within their own hearts."
I have seen it. Furthermore, from a verse: "The Patriarch’s Three Great Treatises—how profound is the intent behind leaving them as a gift!

When I unroll the scrolls and am confused by the text, I burn incense and seek it within the Great Canon. Although these annotations are small in form, they are not merely a labor of the mind. I vow that by this merit..."
He returned with the resources to build the Seven-Jeweled Grove.

In the postscript, he discusses the teachings of our ancestor, the Dharma Master Zhiyi, in three sections. Their purport is profound and far-reaching; their phrasing is vast and expansive. Were it not for one whose insight penetrates...
Heavenly Man! Your wisdom encompasses both the present and the past; it is not easy to fathom the depths of what you harbor within.

Since I began my travels and studies at Mount Danqiu, I have often heard that Dharma Master Chuan’an grows ever more venerable in years and ever more eminent in virtue. His insight is clear and far-reaching, and he has attained a uniquely realized learning transmitted directly from mind to mind.
He constantly reaches the transcendent heights of the ancients; even those renowned scholars who appear only once in a generation often...
None could equal him on his right. Observing his character, he was fond of learning without weariness and delighted in teaching without fatigue;

possessing both benevolence and wisdom in perfect measure, he was a rarity in this world. From dawn till dusk, he never slackened in his efforts to mold and cultivate those who came late to his guidance, ensuring that every person returned to the standard of his model.
His resolve may truly be called ultimate. Yet the Master still considered this insufficient; regarding his lectures and instructions—
Beyond this, I have annotated the texts of the three divisions [of the *Mohe zhiguan*], clarifying what was doubtful and illuminating what was obscure.

Thus, may the teaching of our Patriarch be like the blue sky and the bright sun, such that all people know its clarity and purity; may it be like the phoenix and the magical herb, such that all people know them to be auspicious omens.
To assist and support our teaching—how could this assistance be considered small? Therefore, these four fascicles of *Zhizhi guan* are titled *Zulan* (Aids for Surveying). I...
When he returned to his hometown later in life, the Master had already passed away. Fearing constantly that these writings might be lost to oblivion, he kept this concern in mind both day and night.
By chance, when he spoke of this collection to the scholar Pan, explaining how it would benefit the world, Pan agreed to encourage its carving onto printing blocks for circulation.
Pan followed his lead with great resolve, saying, "I do not dare seek even the slightest profit from this; rather, I wish to make it convenient for scholars to copy and study."

This labor also serves to widely disseminate the teachings of the Dharma Master. I have further encouraged his resolve and thus appended this letter to the head seat Bai-lan at Tiantai, seeking a draft copy.
Master Zhang rejoices in perfecting the excellence of others and delights in extolling their virtues;
he always takes the propagation of the Way as his heart’s concern. Upon reading my letter, he immediately visited Acharya Yi. As for Master Yi—
This is indeed the legacy of the Dharma Master. It is not merely that he delights in my writings and wishes to provide their original texts;

it is also his way of repaying the kindness of his former teacher. Alas! From this day forward, the teaching of the Dharma Master shall be transmitted forever without decay, and his fame shall resound through the ages.
Beholding these writings, I am overcome with joy and have thus hastily composed this preface to follow after them.
Preface by the Dharma-transmitting Śramaṇa Shenhui, Abbot of Xianlin Monastery in Hengyang, Yongjia, on the [blank] day of the second month in the fourth year of the Zhenghe era.
